title: Gas exchange, gas transport and control of breathing
blurb: Explain how O₂ and CO₂ cross membranes, how blood carries each one, and what tells you to breathe.
question: During a panic attack a student breathes fast and deep for several minutes. What happens to the CO₂ level and pH of her blood, and which part of the brain normally sets her breathing rhythm?

teach.body: Formally, external respiration is gas exchange between the alveoli and the blood in the lung capillaries; internal respiration is gas exchange between the blood and the tissue cells. Both happen by simple diffusion down partial-pressure gradients. Cellular respiration is a different process: making ATP in the mitochondria. In plain English: oxygen gets loaded in the lungs, unloaded at the tissues, then burned for energy inside the cells.

teach.caption: Neither uses ATP: each gas simply moves from where its partial pressure is higher to where it is lower.
External respiration happens at 1, the lung capillaries; internal respiration happens at 2, the body-tissue capillaries. Note that O₂-poor blood reaches the lungs in the pulmonary artery.

teach.h: Down the gradient, no energy needed
teach.body: Each gas diffuses from higher to lower partial pressure. In the lungs, O₂ is high in the alveoli and lower in the arriving blood, so it moves into the blood; CO₂ is high in the blood, so it moves into the alveoli. At the tissues the gradients reverse. The respiratory membrane (alveolar wall plus capillary wall) is very thin, so diffusion is fast.

items.label: O₂ molecules per hemoglobin, at most

teach.caption: CO₂ bound to hemoglobin is called carbaminohemoglobin.

teach.body: Inside red blood cells, the enzyme carbonic anhydrase speeds this reversible reaction: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid) ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ (bicarbonate). Most bicarbonate then travels in the plasma. In the lungs the reaction runs backward and CO₂ is released to be exhaled. Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it binds hemoglobin far more strongly than O₂, blocking oxygen transport.

head: Structure
Location
Role
rows: Sense CO₂ as CSF pH falls

teach.caption: In a healthy person, rising CO₂ (not low O₂) is the strongest everyday drive to breathe.

teach.body: Priya, a nursing applicant, hyperventilates during a panic attack before her TEAS. She blows off CO₂, so less carbonic acid forms and her blood pH rises: respiratory alkalosis. On a clinic shadow shift she meets Mr. Walker, heavily sedated after surgery, breathing slowly and shallowly. He is hypoventilating: CO₂ builds up, more H⁺ forms and his blood pH falls: respiratory acidosis.

teach.text: Two transport reversals catch people: O₂ travels mostly BOUND TO HEMOGLOBIN (not dissolved), and CO₂ travels mostly as BICARBONATE (not on hemoglobin). And the breathing centers sit in the brainstem (medulla and pons), not the cerebrum or cerebellum.

items: External respiration: lungs; internal respiration: tissues; both by simple diffusion.
O₂: about 98.5% on hemoglobin (up to 4 O₂ each), about 1.5% dissolved.
CO₂: about 70% bicarbonate, 20–23% on hemoglobin, 7–10% dissolved.
Carbonic anhydrase in RBCs: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻.
Medulla sets the rhythm, pons smooths it; rising CO₂ is the main drive.
Hypoventilation: respiratory acidosis. Hyperventilation: respiratory alkalosis.

summary: You can now tell external, internal and cellular respiration apart, explain diffusion down partial-pressure gradients, and state how blood carries O₂ and CO₂. You can also explain how the medulla, pons and chemoreceptors control breathing and predict the pH effect of over- or under-breathing.

A.q: How is most of the oxygen in arterial blood transported?
A.why: About 98.5% of oxygen is carried bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells as oxyhemoglobin; only about 1.5% is dissolved.

whyNot.0: Only about 1.5% of O₂ travels dissolved in plasma.
whyNot.1: Bicarbonate is how most CO₂ is carried, not O₂.
whyNot.3: Albumin maintains osmotic pressure; it is not the oxygen carrier.

A.q: Where is the basic rhythm of breathing generated?
A.why: The respiratory centers in the medulla oblongata set the rhythm; the pons smooths the pattern.

whyNot.1: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance, not breathing rhythm.
whyNot.2: The hypothalamus is not the respiratory rhythm center; that is in the brainstem.
whyNot.3: The cerebral cortex allows voluntary control, such as holding your breath, but does not generate the automatic rhythm.

A.q: In a healthy person at rest, which change is the strongest stimulus to increase breathing?
A.why: Rising CO₂, sensed as falling pH in the CSF by central chemoreceptors in the medulla, is the strongest everyday drive to breathe.

whyNot.0: Low O₂ is sensed by peripheral chemoreceptors, but it is not the main drive in a healthy person.
whyNot.2: A rise in pH (more alkaline) would slow breathing, not speed it up.
whyNot.3: Falling CO₂ reduces the drive to breathe.

B.q: About 70% of the carbon dioxide in blood is carried as:
B.why: Most CO₂ (about 70%) is converted by carbonic anhydrase and carried as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) in the plasma.

whyNot.0: Carbaminohemoglobin (CO₂ on hemoglobin) carries only about 20–23%.
whyNot.1: Dissolved CO₂ accounts for only about 7–10%.
whyNot.2: Carbonic acid is a short-lived step; it quickly splits into H⁺ and bicarbonate.

B.q: Internal respiration is best described as:
options: Gas exchange between the alveoli and the blood
Gas exchange between blood and tissue cells
Using O₂ to make ATP inside mitochondria
Movement of air into and out of the lungs
B.why: Internal respiration is the exchange of O₂ and CO₂ between systemic capillary blood and the tissue cells.

whyNot.0: Exchange between alveoli and blood is EXTERNAL respiration.
whyNot.2: Making ATP in mitochondria is cellular respiration, a separate process.
whyNot.3: Moving air in and out is pulmonary ventilation (breathing).

B.q: The peripheral chemoreceptors that respond mainly to low blood oxygen are located in the:
B.why: Peripheral chemoreceptors sit in the carotid and aortic bodies and respond to low O₂ (and to CO₂ and H⁺).

whyNot.1: The medulla houses the CENTRAL chemoreceptors, which respond to CO₂ via CSF pH.
whyNot.2: Alveolar walls are the exchange surface; they do not hold the chemoreceptors.
whyNot.3: The pulmonary veins and left atrium carry blood; they are not chemoreceptor sites.

C.q: A student breathes rapidly and deeply during a panic attack. Which outcome is expected?
C.why: Hyperventilation blows off CO₂, so less carbonic acid forms, H⁺ falls and pH rises: respiratory alkalosis.

whyNot.1: Losing CO₂ lowers acid, so pH rises; acidosis would need CO₂ to build up.
whyNot.2: Retaining CO₂ causes acidosis, but hyperventilation removes CO₂ rather than retaining it.
whyNot.3: CO₂ retention lowers pH; it cannot cause alkalosis, and fast breathing does not retain CO₂.

C.q: Carbon monoxide poisoning reduces oxygen delivery to tissues mainly because carbon monoxide:
options: Binds plasma albumin in place of O₂
Raises blood CO₂ so the pH falls
Binds hemoglobin far more strongly than O₂
Destroys type II cells, so alveoli collapse
C.why: CO binds hemoglobin far more strongly than O₂, taking up the sites oxygen would use, so less O₂ is carried.

whyNot.0: Oxygen is not carried on albumin, so CO taking its place there would not matter.
whyNot.1: CO and CO₂ are different gases; carbon monoxide's harm is blocking hemoglobin.
whyNot.3: Carbon monoxide does not act by destroying surfactant cells; it blocks hemoglobin.

C.q: Which statement about external respiration is CORRECT?
options: O₂ moves alveoli to blood by active transport
CO₂ moves alveoli to blood by simple diffusion
O₂ moves bronchioles to blood by diffusion
O₂ moves alveoli to blood by simple diffusion
C.why: In the lungs O₂ diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, down its partial-pressure gradient, with no ATP needed.

whyNot.0: Gas exchange uses simple diffusion, not active transport.
whyNot.1: CO₂ moves the other way in the lungs: from blood into the alveoli.
whyNot.2: Bronchioles are conducting airways; exchange happens across the alveolar wall.

reteach.title: Gases leave crowded rooms
reteach.question: Picture people leaving a packed room through an open door into an almost empty hallway. How is that like oxygen and carbon dioxide moving in the lungs and tissues?

blocks.body: Nobody has to push a crowd out of a packed room: people drift toward the emptier hallway on their own. Gases do the same. Partial pressure is how "crowded" a gas is. O₂ is crowded in the alveoli, so it drifts into the blood; at the tissues, O₂ is crowded in the blood, so it drifts into cells. CO₂ is crowded in the cells and drifts the opposite way. No energy is spent: that is simple diffusion.

Breathing control works like a thermostat set for CO₂. When CO₂ rises (the room gets "too hot"), chemoreceptors in the medulla notice the falling pH and the medulla turns up breathing until CO₂ drops back. Breathe too fast and CO₂ falls too low, pH rises, and you get respiratory alkalosis.

blocks.text: The thermostat reads CO₂, not O₂: in a healthy person, rising CO₂ is the main signal to breathe.

explain.body: External respiration: alveoli and blood exchange gases. Internal respiration: blood and tissue cells exchange gases. Both use simple diffusion. Cellular respiration: making ATP inside mitochondria.

test.q: Which process takes place inside the mitochondria rather than across a capillary wall?
test.why: Cellular respiration uses O₂ to make ATP inside mitochondria; the other processes move gases or air.

whyNot.0: Internal respiration is gas exchange across systemic capillary walls.
whyNot.2: External respiration is gas exchange across the alveolar and capillary walls in the lungs.
whyNot.3: Pulmonary ventilation is moving air in and out of the lungs.

explain.body: About 98.5% of O₂ is bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells (oxyhemoglobin); each hemoglobin carries up to 4 O₂. About 1.5% is dissolved in plasma.

test.q: What is the maximum number of O₂ molecules one hemoglobin molecule can carry?
test.why: Each hemoglobin molecule can carry up to 4 O₂ molecules.

whyNot.0: One is too few; hemoglobin can bind up to four O₂.
whyNot.1: Two is too few; hemoglobin can bind up to four O₂.
whyNot.2: Eight is double the real maximum of four.

explain.body: About 70% of CO₂ travels as bicarbonate. Carbonic anhydrase in red cells speeds CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. About 20–23% rides on hemoglobin (carbaminohemoglobin) and 7–10% is dissolved.

test.q: Inside red blood cells, which enzyme speeds the conversion of CO₂ and water into carbonic acid?
test.why: Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃, the first step toward bicarbonate.

whyNot.1: Carbaminohemoglobin is CO₂ bound to hemoglobin, not an enzyme.
whyNot.2: Erythropoietin is a kidney hormone that stimulates RBC production.
whyNot.3: Oxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin carrying O₂, not an enzyme.

explain.body: The medulla sets the rhythm and the pons smooths it. Rising CO₂ is the main drive. Hypoventilation lets CO₂ build up and pH fall (respiratory acidosis); hyperventilation blows CO₂ off and pH rises (respiratory alkalosis).

test.q: After heavy sedation, a patient breathes slowly and shallowly for an hour. Which change in the blood is expected?
test.why: Hypoventilation retains CO₂, which forms more carbonic acid and H⁺, so pH falls: respiratory acidosis.

whyNot.0: Falling CO₂ and rising pH is what hyperventilation causes.
whyNot.1: More CO₂ means more H⁺, so pH falls rather than rises.
whyNot.3: Slow, shallow breathing retains CO₂; it does not lower it.
